query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for high-temperature applications, the high configurational entropy drives a selective surface segregation of oxidation‐active elements (e.g. Cr and Al) during early exposure to oxygen, leading to the rapid formation of a continuous and adherent protective oxide layer (such as a Cr‐ or Al‐rich oxide, e.g. CrTaO4 or Al2O3) that retards further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized single‐phase or dual‐phase HEA (e.g. one formulated with significant Cr and Al content) produced by conventional processing (such as vacuum arc melting) that exhibits a uniform microstructure prior to oxidation.
generation.intervention: Expose HEA specimens with controlled variations in the content of oxidation‐active elements to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (e.g. air at 1000°C) for extended durations.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests conducted in air at temperatures between 900°C and 1100°C for durations up to 200 hours, ensuring similar initial microstructures and grain sizes.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, dense oxide scale enriched in special elements (e.g. Cr- or Al-rich oxides such as CrTaO4-based or Al2O3 layers) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy retards bulk diffusion but facilitates selective surface segregation of elements with a high affinity for oxygen. These elements then rapidly oxidize to form a thin, adherent, and protective oxide layer that acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA samples with higher concentrations of oxidation-active elements are expected to develop an oxide layer that is thinner, more continuous, and less porous, showing lower mass gains and improved oxidation resistance compared to alloys with a more uniform distribution of elements.
generation.baseline: Control HEAs with reduced or less segregating concentrations of oxidation-active elements, which would form thicker, less adherent and more porous oxide scales with higher mass gains under the same oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold at high temperatures (approximately 900–1100°C) over extended exposure (up to 200 hours) and for alloys with similar processing histories; deviations in processing, microstructural scale, or testing atmospheres may lead to variations in the observed behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trend is supported by observed oxide protective behavior in several high-entropy systems, the quantitative balance between diffusion retardation by entropy and segregation kinetics remains uncertain. Additionally, the influence of minor elements and local microstructural features may modify the oxide growth dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with an increased concentration of oxidation-active elements (e.g., higher Cr/Al content) and one with these elements reduced or uniformly distributed. Subject both sets to identical isothermal oxidation treatments at 1000°C in air for 200 hours. Monitor the oxidation progression in situ (e.g., via high-temperature X-ray diffraction) and perform post-test analyses (SEM, EDS/XPS, and mass gain measurements).
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time
Oxide layer thickness and morphology via SEM
Phase identification of the oxide scale via XRD
Elemental distribution at the surface via EDS or XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples enriched in oxidation-active elements do not form a thinner, more continuous, and protective oxide layer (i.e., they show similar or higher mass gains, thicker or more porous oxide layers, or lack evidence of selective segregation compared to the control samples), then the hypothesis that selective segregation driven by configurational entropy is the primary mechanism for protective oxide formation is falsified.

Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C

Abstract: AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. High-Temperature Oxidation Behavior of AlTiNiCuCox High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: In this study, the high-temperature oxidation behavior of a series of AlTiNiCuCox high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was explored. The AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5) series HEAs were prepared using a vacuum induction melting furnace, in which three kinds of AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) alloys with different Co contents were oxidized at 800 °C for 100 h, and their oxidation kinetic curves were determined. The microstructure, morphology, structure, and phase composition of the oxide film surface and cross-sectional layers of AlTiNiCuCox series HEAs were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The influence of Co content on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEAs was discussed, and the oxidation mechanism was summarized. The results indicate that, at 800 °C, the AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) series HEAs had dense oxide films and certain high-temperature oxidation resistance.
